newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed says govt trying to muzzle media.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed says govt trying to muzzle media.

text.p: Russia's former security chief and would-be president Alexander Lebed accused the government on Friday of trying to stifle press freedom.
"Power in Russia has finally turned into a structure of rigid hierarchy and the mass media is in opposition and is no longer needed by the authorities," Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying.
The popular reserve general, sacked by President Boris Yeltsin as Russia's security chief last autumn, said the mass media was falling under the tight control of a small group of financiers.

Echoing other opposition politicians, Lebed said the financiers were in turn beholden to First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, drafted into the government by Yeltsin last month to speed up economic reforms.
Yeltsin said earlier this month that the independence of the media was one of the biggest gains of democratic Russia and that he would protect it.
A government spokesmen took up the same theme this week, but at the same time criticised a host of publications for stories which he said were incorrect.

The debate over press freedom in Russia intensified this week when the communist-dominated State Duma -- lower house of parliament -- decided to set strict limits on television coverage of its sessions.

The Duma's decision followed months of complaints by opposition deputies that newspapers and television have become political weapons in the hands of the state, a few rich entrepreneurs and major companies which are their shareholders.
Lebed condemned the Duma move as "indisputable stupidity".
The gruff ex-soldier, who does not hide his ambition to succeed Yeltsin as president one day, said his newly formed Russian Popular Republican Party had been formally registered on Friday.
He said it already had 15,000 members in 78 regions around the country.
